text: Which project set out to backhaul dense 5G small cells by exploiting the millimetre wave spectrum above 100 GHz, combining D-band point-to-multipoint coverage with G-band point-to-point feeder links and using newly designed traveling wave tubes to provide the transmission power?
reference_answer: ULTRAWAVE. It proposed exploiting the whole millimetre wave spectrum beyond 100 GHz to create an ultra-capacity backhaul layer for dense 5G small cells, targeting more than 100 Gbps per kilometre square in point-to-multipoint at D-band (141 - 174.8 GHz) over a 500 m radius of coverage, fed by novel G-band (300 GHz) point-to-point links with more than 600 m range; Watt-level transmission power came from two newly designed traveling wave tube amplifiers, one at D-band and one at G-band, converged with solid-state electronics and photonics.

text: Cheap ceramic magnets made from iron oxide are much weaker than the high-performance magnets that rely on hard-to-source imported metals. How do the EU-funded projects working to make the iron-oxide kind strong enough to take their place differ in their approaches?
reference_answer: Two projects take this on from opposite ends. AMPHIBIAN works at the materials level: it builds hybrid magnets that couple hard ferrite to a soft magnetic phase through magnetostatic interactions (patent P201600092), targeting up-scalable, cost-efficient fabrication of dense anisotropic ferrite-based magnets with 40% enhanced magnetic performance (energy products above 55 kJ/m3) over commercial ferrites; it reports a 40% increase in energy product, 50 kg of SrFe12O19-Fe hybrid magnets fabricated by Max Baermann, and a completely rare-earth-free flywheel as its substitution demonstrator. PASSENGER works at the industrial end, scaling improved strontium ferrite (Sr-ferrite) up a pilot line: 4 tones of improved Sr-ferrite were industrially produced in the first 18 months, and its report states that improving ferrite 'with no use of any critical raw material' overcame one of the main limitations of ferrite magnets, 'the risk that magnets might become demagnetized when operating in cold environments (below 0 C)', which matters for e-mobility in cold conditions. Its 8 innovative pilot plants at TRL 7 aim at up-scaled production (several tonnes per year) of REE-free permanent magnets with a major cost advantage by comparison NdFeB magnets, demonstrated in electromobility applications and water motor pumps, with the consortium given in its final report as 21 partners (14 companies) from 8 countries; the same programme also runs a manganese-aluminium-carbon (MnAlC) line, which is context for the project rather than part of the iron-oxide answer. The contrast is therefore one composite-magnet concept carried from proof-of-concept to a single energy-storage demonstrator, against an industrial scale-up of ferrite itself to pilot-plant volumes and vehicle-grade robustness.
notes: Seeds: 720853 AMPHIBIAN and 101003914 PASSENGER, reached from corpus-profile candidate vector-11 (rare-earth-free permanent magnets); the candidate's own sample ids 686056 NOVAMAG and 636876 REDMUD were read first and both fall outside this question (NOVAMAG designs new RE-free/lean intermetallic phases by computational screening, no iron-oxide magnet line; REDMUD recovers rare earths from bauxite residue). Question deliberately narrowed to the iron-oxide/ferrite substitution line: the broader reading 'permanent magnets free of critical metals' has 5 satisfying projects (NOVAMAG, AMPHIBIAN, PASSENGER, 691235 INAPEM, 757333 SpdTuM) and would be L3. The 'iron-oxide kind' clause is load-bearing and must not be widened. Reference scope: the answer elements are ferrite-only on both sides - AMPHIBIAN's ferrite composite work and PASSENGER's Sr-ferrite pilot line (4 tones produced in 18 months, the below-0 C demagnetisation fix, TRL 7 pilot plants, electromobility and water motor pumps); PASSENGER's MnAlC strand is named only as programme context and is not required of an answer, since MnAlC is an intermetallic and this question's boundary excludes intermetallic routes (NOVAMAG, SpdTuM, INAPEM). Partner counts: PASSENGER's objective says '13 industrial partners' from 8 EU countries while its finalResults says 'The consortium consists of 21 partners (14 companies) from 8 countries'; the reference quotes the finalResults figure and says so. text: How have EU-funded businesses tried to earn money by bringing older people who feel lonely together with other people in person?
reference_answer: Two EU-funded ventures sell company itself rather than a device. The Freebird Club (FreeBC_Orgs) runs a membership-based peer-to-peer social travel and homestay club exclusively for older adults: members travel and stay with each other for a nightly rate inside a trusted community of senior peers, so a host earns income while both sides get companionship, and the project extended the club from individual to organisational membership so age-sector bodies could bring in the 'harder to reach' seniors - piloted by bringing a group of 12 older adults from the London Irish Centre's Senior Wellbeing Service to stay with local hosts in Kerry, Ireland. ADOPT GRANDPARENTS works in the opposite direction, pairing elderly people living in care homes with youngsters for supervised shared visits and activities under a Social & Education Training Programme; after three years as a non-profit, Intergenerational Technologies SL was constituted as a company to run it as a social economy business, launched in Spain and Portugal and projecting growth to 242 employees and EUR 23,017,094 revenues by 2024. Both frame loneliness in later life as the market: Freebird also targets financial insecurity and the lack of travel options for seniors, while ADOPT GRANDPARENTS also aims at the loss of intergenerational contact for the young.
